record.paper_title: Research Problems on Relations Between Nijenhuis Geometry and Integrable Systems
record.original_question: Can two distinct third-order Poisson structures be compatible when at least one of them is non-Darboux–Poisson, and more generally how large can a pencil of first-order geometric Poisson structures compatible with a non-Darboux–Poisson third-order structure be?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.5. Can two different Poisson structures of order 3, one of which is not Darboux-Poisson, be compatible?

Problem 6.6. Describe all geometric Poisson structures of the first order compatible with a geometric Poisson structure of the third order which is not Darboux-Poisson. How big can the compatible pencil of such first order structures be?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a smooth manifold $M$ with local coordinates $u^1,\dots,u^n$. A homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structure of order $k$ is a Poisson bracket on the loop space of $M$ given, on local functionals, by an operator of the form
$$P^{ij} = \sum_{s=0}^{k} A^{ij}_s(u,u_x,u_{xx},\dots)\,\partial_x^{\,k-s},$$
whose leading coefficient and lower-order coefficients depend polynomially on the jets in such a way that $P$ is homogeneous of weight $k$ (with $\deg \partial_x = 1$ and $\deg u^i_{(\ell)} = \ell$) and skew-symmetric, and such that the associated bracket $\{F,G\} = \int \frac{\delta F}{\delta u^i} P^{ij} \frac{\delta G}{\delta u^j}\,dx$ satisfies the Jacobi identity. Two such structures $P_1, P_2$ are called compatible if every linear combination $\lambda P_1 + \mu P_2$ is again a Poisson structure; the family $\{\lambda P_1+\mu P_2\}$ is then called a (Poisson) pencil. A third-order Poisson structure is said to be Darboux–Poisson if there exist local coordinates in which all of its coefficients are constant (so it reduces to $c^{ij}\partial_x^3$ with $c^{ij}$ constant skew-symmetric).

Problems.
(a) Do there exist two distinct (i.e., non-proportional) compatible third-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures on some manifold $M$ such that at least one of them is not Darboux–Poisson? If yes, classify such pairs; if no, prove that compatibility of two third-order structures forces both to be Darboux–Poisson (up to a common change of coordinates).

(b) Given a third-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structure $P_3$ on $M$ that is not Darboux–Poisson, describe all first-order homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures $P_1$ (i.e., Hamiltonian operators of hydrodynamic type) that are compatible with $P_3$. In particular, determine the maximal possible dimension of a linear pencil of such first-order structures compatible with $P_3$.
artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not surface any publication resolving the compatibility question for higher-order (specifically third-order) homogeneous differential-geometric Poisson structures with at least one being non-Darboux–Poisson, nor a classification of first-order Poisson pencils compatible with a non-Darboux–Poisson third-order structure. The problems appear to remain open as posed in the broader Nijenhuis-geometry/integrable-systems literature.

status_evidence.title: Lie algebras with compatible scalar products for non-homogeneous Hamiltonian operators
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses compatibility of Hamiltonian operators of different orders but does not classify third-order non-Darboux–Poisson compatible pairs.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work on compatibility of higher-order Hamiltonian operators does not resolve the stated problems.

status_evidence.title: Poisson pencils: reduction, exactness, and invariants
status_evidence.snippet: Treats Poisson pencils and bi-Hamiltonian deformations but addresses compatibility with first-order (hydrodynamic-type) leading terms, not non-Darboux–Poisson third-order structures.
status_evidence.claim: General Poisson-pencil literature does not contain the requested description.
